body:
## Problem

`vim.pack` uses a private async implementation even though `vim.async` is now available.

## Solution

Remove the private implementation and run parallel plugin operations as structured child tasks. Bound concurrency with semaphores, use protected awaits to isolate recoverable failures without swallowing task cancellation.

comment_data.body:
It feels wrong that `async.run` needs to be nested 3 times (not to mention the `semaphore` + `pawait`, which are their own closures, thus 5 total nesting levels here). 

This is basically the feedback I had in https://github.com/lewis6991/async.nvim/issues/24 . I'm sure there's technical reasons for the current situation, but it just feels really wrong. Task chaining should reduce nesting, yet we have actually increased nesting here.

And this is not merely about "readability"; it's actually hard to write this.

Why can't we do this (pseudocode, no idea if this "makes sense", but the point is that there should be ~one "entry point" for creating tasks, not 5 nested levels):

```lua
        async.run({ semaphore=(2*cpu), pawait=true}, function()
```

...instead of this:

```lua
        async.run(function()
          -- A failed lookup should not cancel sibling lookups.
          semaphore:with(function()
            async.pawait(async.run(function()
```

(The lower-level things can still be available for the "uncommon case". The common case should be obvious and ergonomic, not 3+ nesting levels.)

comment_data.body:
We need at least two levels, one for the top level parent task, and the second level for the child tasks which are bound to the parent. Hopefully you don't see a problem with this.

The extra level is unfortunate but is needed to use the semaphore properly. I'll see if we can improve this.

This line specifically needs an extra `async.run()` for the exact reason I explained [here](https://github.com/neovim/neovim/pull/41674#discussion_r3929211324), otherwise we would use `pcall`.

comment_data.body:
There are genuine technical reasons for writing the code like this. If the nesting is really that bad the alternative is:

```lua
  local function add_p_data_info(p_data_list, offline)
    local plug_dir = get_plug_dir()
    async
      .run(function()
        local semaphore = async.semaphore(2 * (uv.available_parallelism() or 1))

        for _, p_data in ipairs(p_data_list) do
          local plug = new_plug(p_data.spec, plug_dir)
          local path = p_data.path

          async.run(function()
            copcall(semaphore.with, semaphore, function()
              p_data.branches = git_get_branches(path)
              p_data.tags = git_get_tags(path)
              p_data.manifest = manifest_read(path)

              if not offline then
                git_fetch(path)
              end

              infer_revisions(plug)
              p_data.rev = plug.info.sha_head
              p_data.rev_to = plug.info.sha_target
            end)

            async.checkpoint()
          end)
        end
      end)
      :wait(max_timeout)
  end
```

Note the main different here is the inclusion of a `async.checkpoint()` call. In the other version this wasn't needed since we were using `async.pawait(async.run(...))` instead.

Personally I don't think this is much better.

comment_data.body:
Also worth noting that the previous code already had most of these layers, but hid them inside `async_join_run_wait()` and `async.join()`. This change makes the task scope and bounded worker concurrency explicit through the semaphore.

Since the top level task is immediately waited and not returned, if we want we could actually change the `async.pawait(async.run())` into normal `pcall` since nothing is exposed to cancel any tasks, but I'm not sure if that's a good practice to follow.

kwargs is fine and actually what I've tried to implement for things it makes sense for. However I have explicitly avoided this if it can dynamically change the signature of the call as that breaks typing.

For `protected` I would avoid since this does change the signature.

For `semaphore` I'm not sure this makes sense as you need to have some sort of boundary where the semaphore is acquired and released.

comment_data.body:
> I think the helper was a bit contrived, obfuscated the logic and didn't necessarily make things easier to understand. The `async.run` calls explicitly mark were the asynchronous boundaries are.

I think I don't agree, at least for these reasons:

- It executes code with `wait()`, so when called it is treated the same as regular synchronous function. Which is the main point here.
- The name `async_*` is enough to understand that this does the "async" part inside.
- It increases the amount of nesting/indentation which is what makes things harder (at least for me) to understand and reason about.
- It increases the diff.

If it is technically possible (and I'd assume it should be since `vim.async` is more capable than `vim._async`), I'd keep the helper approach.

comment_data.body:
Thinking about this we could allow passing a semaphore to `async.run()` which then acts as the boundary.

```lua
async.run(function()  -- top level - needed
  local semaphore = async.semaphore(n)

  for f in funcs do
    async.run({ semaphore = semaphore }, function() -- child - needed
        async.pawait(async.run(f))  -- basically pcall(f)
    end)
  end

  -- vim.async asynchronously waits here until all children have finished.
end)
```

If we wanted to reduce this further then we'd need to add something like `async.prun` (protected version of `async.run`). Note this wouldn't be the same as `async.pcall()` which I suggested in the other PR as `prun` would be non-blocking and return a task.


```lua
async.run(function()
  local semaphore = async.semaphore(n)

  for f in funcs do
    async.prun({ semaphore = semaphore }, f)
  end
end)
```

The semaphore thing is probably worth doing. Not so sure about `prun`.

comment_data.body:
Yeah maybe, little worried it may be over optimizing the API for this specific use case. The previous version of this change with `vim._async` was code-golfed quite a bit, so I'm wary the diff is misleading.

Just to clarify in case there's any confusion:
- `async.prun` - protected version of `async.run`, returns a Task, **sync & non-blocking**
- `async.pcall` (mentioned in other PR) - returns function results (pcall style), **async & blocking**. Sugar for `async.pawait(async.run(...))`

I've changed the PR back to the old style so all the extra nesting is hidden like before.

comment_regular_data.body:
related: #41645

When done, can we get some performance measurements? This would let us know if #41674 would even be necessary.

> related: #41645
> 
> When done, can we get some performance measurements? This would let us know if #41674 would even be necessary.

I don’t think benchmarking would be particularly meaningful here. `vim.pack` is already asynchronous; this PR primarily replaces the temporary `vim._async` implementation with `vim.async` while preserving the existing concurrency.

In practice, `vim.pack` is dominated by filesystem, process, and network I/O, so results would be highly environment-dependent. A synthetic  benchmark could isolate scheduler overhead, but that overhead should be negligible relative to the work `vim.pack` performs.
